title: Section 164 CrPC Statement and Retraction Law
metaTitle: Section 164 CrPC Statement and Retraction Law
metaDescription: Understand Section 164 CrPC confessions vs Section 161 police statements in Bangladesh, magistrate safeguards, Evidence Act rules, and retraction steps.
heroIntro: Under Section 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure 1898, only a Judicial Magistrate may record a voluntary confessional statement of an accused or an eyewitness statement during investigation, following mandatory Section 364 safeguards. Involuntary confessions extracted via torture are inadmissible under Evidence Act Section 24 and may be retracted.

sections.title: Legal Distinction Between Section 161 and Section 164 CrPC
sections.content:
A Section 164 statement is a formal judicial record recorded by a Magistrate, whereas a Section 161 note is an unsigned police investigation memorandum. Under Section 161 CrPC and Section 162 CrPC, statements made to investigating police during FIR investigation are inadmissible as substantive evidence and may only be used to contradict a prosecution witness at trial.

In sharp contrast, Section 164 empowers a Judicial Magistrate to record both witness depositions and accused confessions while an inquiry is ongoing. Because Section 25 of the Evidence Act 1872 strictly bars confessions made to police, investigating officers frequently request remand to pressure suspects before producing them in chamber.

FeatureSection 161 CrPCSection 164 CrPC
Recording AuthorityPolice Investigating OfficerJudicial / Metropolitan Magistrate
Signature RequirementProhibited under Sec. 162 CrPCMandatory under Sec. 364 CrPC
Evidentiary ValueContradiction only (Sec. 145 Evidence Act)Substantive evidence if voluntary (Sec. 80)
Voluntariness SafeguardsNone formally recordedSec. 164(3) warning & reflection period

Understanding these boundaries alongside police remand legal limits protects suspects against unlawful custodial self-incrimination during police questioning.

sections.title: Mandatory Magistrate Safeguards Under Sections 164 and 364
sections.content:
Before recording a confession under Section 164(3) CrPC, the Magistrate must independently verify that no police coercion, threat, or inducement taints the accused's free will. If mandatory procedural steps under Sections 164 and 364 are violated in a manner that prejudices defense rights and cannot be cured under Section 533 CrPC, the confession collapses legally at trial.

Specifically, the recording Magistrate must remove all police personnel from the chamber, grant adequate quiet reflection time (customarily at least three hours free from police custody), inspect physical marks of torture, question how long the suspect remained in police custody, and explicitly warn the accused that they are not bound to confess and that any statement will be used in evidence against them.

Moreover, under Section 364 CrPC, every question and answer must be recorded in full in the accused's own language and read back before signing. Where warrantless arrest rules or custodial safeguards were breached prior to chamber production, defense counsel must highlight those time gaps immediately during bail hearings under Section 497 CrPC.

sections.title: How to Retract a Coerced Section 164 Confession
sections.content:
An accused who confessed under police torture, intimidation, or false promises of release can file a formal retraction petition before the trial court. Under Section 24 of the Evidence Act 1872, any confession appearing to be caused by inducement, threat, or promise from a person in authority is completely irrelevant in criminal proceedings.

  1. Report Custodial Abuse Immediately: Inform the Magistrate or jail doctor at the first opportunity after leaving police remand so medical injuries are officially logged.
  2. File a Written Retraction Petition: Submit an immediate application through defense counsel stating exact dates of remand, coercion methods, and repudiating the statement as untrue and involuntary.
  3. Demand Medical and Custody Records: Petition the court to summon jail admission registers, General Diary entries, and remand forwarding memos showing injuries or custody delays.
  4. Cross-Examine the Recording Magistrate: During trial, scrutinize noncompliance with reflection time, absence of mandatory warnings, or verbatim mismatch under Section 364 CrPC, alongside independent grounds for High Court quashing under Section 561A CrPC.

Even against co-accused, Section 30 of the Evidence Act limits how a retracted confession may be weighed without strong independent corroboration.

sections.title: Documents Checklist to Challenge an Involuntary Confession
sections.content:
Objective custody timelines and medical entries carry far stronger weight than bare oral denials when asking a Sessions Judge or High Court bench to discard a Section 164 CrPC confession. Appellate precedents emphasize corroborating custody gaps and custodial injury logs alongside timely retraction. Secure certified copies of these primary records through your defense advocate without delay:

  • Certified copy of the complete Section 164 CrPC recording sheet, including the Magistrate's Section 364 memorandum and exact entry-exit timing stamps.
  • Police remand petition, station forwarding report, and Magistrate's remand order demonstrating the total duration spent under police custody prior to confession.
  • Prison medical officer examination report and jail gate admission register recorded immediately upon return from police remand.
  • Certified First Information Report (FIR), seizure list, and charge sheet showing whether the recorded statement contradicts physical discovery facts under Section 27 of the Evidence Act.
  • Dated written retraction petition lodged promptly before the Chief Judicial Magistrate, Metropolitan Magistrate, or trial Sessions Judge.
  • Records of bail and surety filings or earlier High Court detention petitions challenging unlawful detention or remand irregularities.

sections.title: Criminal Defense Strategy and Chamber Consultation
sections.content:
A recorded Section 164 confession drastically complicates criminal trials—especially when it implicates co-accused under Section 30 of the Evidence Act—unless challenged early and methodically under Section 24 and Sections 164 and 364 CrPC. Waiting until prosecution witness examination concludes before retracting weakens defense credibility; prompt written retraction paired with cross-examination of custody gaps, reflection-period lapses, and independent corroboration failures gives defense counsel maximum strategic leverage in trial and appeal.

faqs.question: Can a police officer record a statement under Section 164 CrPC?
faqs.answer: No. Only a competent Metropolitan Magistrate or Judicial Magistrate of the First Class (or specially empowered Second Class Magistrate) may record a statement under Section 164 CrPC. Statements taken by investigating police officers fall under Section 161 CrPC, cannot be signed, and are barred as confessions by Evidence Act Section 25.

faqs.question: Is a Section 164 confession valid without sufficient reflection time?
faqs.answer: No. Judicial precedent in Bangladesh strictly requires the Magistrate to remove police officers, administer mandatory Section 164(3) warnings, and give the accused calm reflection time—customarily at least three hours—to overcome police fear. Recording a confession immediately after police remand production undermines voluntariness and admissibility at trial.

faqs.question: Can a retracted Section 164 confession still lead to a conviction?
faqs.answer: While a voluntary confession remains admissible under Section 80 of the Evidence Act, settled Appellate Division rulings hold that a retracted confession cannot solely convict the maker without independent material corroboration—and cannot legally be the sole basis to convict any co-accused implicated under Section 30.

faqs.question: When should an accused file a petition to retract a Section 164 confession?
faqs.answer: Retraction should be filed at the earliest possible opportunity—ideally on the very next production date or as soon as legal counsel accesses the accused after remand ends. Prompt written retraction corroborated by jail medical records carries far greater judicial weight than raising coercion months later at trial.

faqs.question: Are Section 164 statements only for accused confessions, or also for witnesses?
faqs.answer: Section 164 CrPC applies to both accused confessions and important witness statements—such as victims in abduction, trafficking, or violent crime cases. Recording an eyewitness statement before a Magistrate under oath helps lock in truthful testimony and deters later witness tampering during trial.
